newsitem.title: CANADA: FORECAST-No relief seen for jobless Canadians. [CORRECTED 20:04 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-No relief seen for jobless Canadians. [CORRECTED 20:04 GMT]

text.p: The army of jobless Canadians, last pegged at more than 1.5 million, faces another tough year in the unemployment line, a Reuters survey of economists shows.

The Reuters quarterly Canadian survey asked 22 economists in Canada and the United States to forecast key economic indicators for the next eight quarters. Some experts opted to forecast only certain items.

The consensus is that the jobless numbers will continue to remain close to the 9- to 10-percent band during the next two years. Canada's current unemployment rate sits at 9.7 percent for December, 1996 (corrects from November) -- a major blot on the economic landscape.
Although all those surveyed agreed unemployment would gradually decline during the next two years, only one of the 22 economists polled predicted a jobless rate under 9.0 percent this year.
"We are not going to have a massive move in the numbers," said Neil Matheson, economist with Standard Life Portfolio Management. "Anything below 9.0 percent is optimistic."
Matheson said the employment picture may be even worse than most people think because Canada's labor participation rate has fallen in the 1990s.
The labor participation rate counts the number of people actively seeking employment in the workforce.
"We've seen a huge pool of people simply drop out of the numbers," Matheson said. "If we had the same participation rate now as we did in 1989, the unemployment rate would be 13 percent."
Many labor experts and economists believe thousands of employable Canadians have given up trying to find jobs and are resigned to remaining on the welfare rolls.
Recent labor statistics add weight to this argument.
Last year, Canada's labor force grew at about 2.0 percent, but the unemployment rate jumped to a high of 10 percent in October.
While U.S. unemployment rates hover in the 5- to 6-percent range, few economists seriously expect Canada's long-term jobless numbers to drop below 8.0 percent.
Inflationary pressures would probably kick in if the country experienced such a drop, Matheson said.
Not all economists are predicting a doom-and-gloom scenario.

With a forecast that unemployment will decline to 8.4 percent by the third quarter of 1998, Mario Angastiniotis, senior economist with MMS International, is the most optimistic forecaster in the survey.
Better-than-expected economic growth is the lynchpin to Angastiniotis' forecast.

The unusually strong pickup in the economy this year will kickstart employment growth later in 1998, and stronger labor participation numbers will not be enough to wipe out the gains, Angastiniotis said.
